Short paper

Hankel Determinants of Geometric Moments and Rational Lambert Values

Erdős #1049 By Will Cook September 2026
PDFOpen the PDF, 20 pages TeXLaTeX source Source on GitHub Problem dossier

Précis. Positive geometric moments and a uniform partition-sum bound give the fixed-base asymptotic of Zudilin’s normalised Hankel determinants, including its constant and power correction. A separate calculation of degrees after cancellation in his 2004 forms extends the rational-base irrationality region. It includes every positive integral power of 31/431/4 and excludes 3/23/2.

This paper owns the fixed-base Hankel asymptotic and rational-base irrationality theorem; the long paper develops exact orders, content and endpoint obstructions, and the remaining problem at 3/23/2.

It is not authority for the validity of claims tagged Lean, which belongs to the cited kernel-checked source, or a solution to Erdős #1049, which remains open.

Authorship and AI use. Will Cook built and directed the research infrastructure and maintains the public release. He reviewed claims when he could. AI agents did most of the research and drafting. Cook did not independently verify every claim.

Cite and contact. Cite this paper by its title, author and date above, with its PDF; cite the earlier sources it uses for a mathematical result. For software, use the release citation and give the commit used. Contact Will with questions or corrections.

We represent 𝑣∗𝑚vm∗ as ∑𝑘≥0𝑎𝑘𝑞(𝑚+1)𝑘∑k≥0akq(m+1)k with 𝑎𝑘 >0ak>0. These are the moments of a positive measure supported on 1,𝑞,𝑞2,…1,q,q2,…. Heine’s identity then expresses the determinant as a sum over choices of 𝑁N nodes, with a squared Vandermonde factor for each choice [7]. The contribution of the first 𝑁N nodes has size 𝑞𝐵𝑁𝑃2𝑁∏𝑘<𝑁𝑎𝑘qBNP2N∏k<Nak up to a positive limiting factor. Moving the last node one place still gives a contribution of comparable size, so we must sum over displaced tuples. We index them by partitions. For each fixed partition, the weight ratios tend to 11; a summable bound independent of 𝑁N then permits passage to the limit in the sum. The resulting limit is the same as for constant weights, for which Cauchy’s determinant formula gives an exact evaluation.

The remaining calculation concerns the weights themselves. Their factorisation involves a two-fold and a three-fold convolution of the sequence 1/(𝑞;𝑞)𝑘1/(q;q)k. Their first relative corrections are −2𝐹(1/𝑞)/(𝑘 +1)−2F(1/q)/(k+1) and −6𝐹(1/𝑞)/(𝑘 +2)−6F(1/q)/(k+2). Adding these corrections and then multiplying the weights over 𝑘 <𝑁k<N gives the power 𝑁−8𝐹(1/𝑞)N−8F(1/q). Theorem 2.1 isolates the determinant argument from this coefficient calculation; it also evaluates the determinant with entries (1 −𝑞𝑖+𝑗+1)−2(1−qi+j+1)−2.

Chowla’s conjecture, recorded by Erdős [1], asks whether 𝐹(𝑡)F(t) is irrational for every rational 𝑡 >1t>1. This is a related arithmetic question, and the fixed-base asymptotic alone does not answer it. In Section 4 we use the different 2004 construction [4] to prove irrationality for coprime 𝑎 >𝑏 ≥1a>b≥1 satisfying

Section 2 proves the general determinant formula. Section 3 constructs the weights and proves Theorem 1.1. The rational-base argument is self-contained in Section 4, with longer calculations and complementary questions linked in Section 5. The additional estimate we need is a growth bound for their coefficients. In that construction the coefficient of 𝐹F before cancellation is a sum of 𝑂(𝑛)O(n) Laurent monomials times two Gaussian binomial polynomials. Each Gaussian polynomial has nonnegative coefficients summing to at most 227𝑛+2227n+2. Thus the sum of the absolute coefficients is exp⁡(𝑂(𝑛))exp⁡(O(n)). Its largest exponent is 𝐾𝑛 =(1091𝑛2 +81𝑛 +2)/2Kn=(1091n2+81n+2)/2, so its absolute value at a fixed 𝑥 >1x>1 is at most 𝑥𝐾𝑛exp⁡(𝑂(𝑛))xKnexp⁡(O(n)). The cyclotomic estimate in the same proof bounds the normalising multiplier by 𝑥𝑊𝑛−𝐾𝑛exp⁡(𝑂𝑥(𝑛))xWn−Knexp⁡(Ox(n)). Multiplication gives

|𝑈𝑛(𝑥)|≤𝑥𝑊𝑛exp⁡(𝑂𝑥(𝑛))(𝑥>1 fixed).|Un(x)|≤xWnexp⁡(Ox(n))(x>1 fixed).

Set 𝜉 =𝐹(𝑎/𝑏)ξ=F(a/b), 𝑄𝑛 =𝑏𝑊𝑛𝑈𝑛(𝑎/𝑏)Qn=bWnUn(a/b) and 𝑃𝑛 =𝑏𝑊𝑛𝑉𝑛(𝑎/𝑏)Pn=bWnVn(a/b). With

For a rational approximation with denominator 𝑞q, we will choose a remainder at most 1/(2𝑞)1/(2q) without letting |𝑄𝑛||Qn| grow unnecessarily. Comparison with earlier criteria

Bundschuh and Väänänen’s Theorem 2 at 𝛼 = −1α=−1 [2] gives irrationality for log⁡𝑏/log⁡𝑎 <𝜃BV :=1/2 −1/𝜋2log⁡b/log⁡a<θBV:=1/2−1/π2. Their 𝑞q is the base 𝑎/𝑏 >1a/b>1, not its reciprocal. Their logarithmic derivative is 𝐿𝑞(𝑧) =∑𝑗≥1(𝑞𝑗 +𝑧)−1Lq(z)=∑j≥1(qj+z)−1, so the value at 𝑧 =𝛼 = −1z=α=−1 is exactly 𝐹(𝑎/𝑏)F(a/b). The rational height is ℎ(𝑞) =𝑎h(q)=a, and their parameter 𝜆 =log⁡ℎ(𝑞)/log⁡𝑞λ=log⁡h(q)/log⁡q is 1/(1 −log⁡𝑏/log⁡𝑎)1/(1−log⁡b/log⁡a), which gives the displayed cutoff. Since 𝜋2 <10π2<10, one has 𝜃BV <2/5 <log⁡4/log⁡31θBV<2/5<log⁡4/log⁡31, so 31/431/4 lies outside that sufficient region. The two sufficient regions differ on [𝜃BV,𝜃∗)[θBV,θ∗). Zudilin also notes an extension to noninteger rational bases 𝑝 =𝑟/𝑠p=r/s for the generalized 𝑞q-logarithm when log⁡|𝑟| >𝑐log⁡|𝑠|log⁡|r|>clog⁡|s|, with 𝑐 >0c>0 computable but unspecified [5]. For 𝐹F, the specialisation above gives 𝑐 =𝜇c=μ, the exponent bound of [4].

The positive-remainder estimates require 𝑥 >1x>1, so they give no statement for negative bases. The series diverges at 𝑥 =1x=1. The companion record also checks the parameters at 7/27/2 in its section on Bundschuh and Väänänen’s height criterion. The analytic irrationality result used there is their cited theorem.

Further questions

An irrationality argument based on these determinants would also require a bound for their coefficient denominators. After clearing them, the nonzero determinants must still tend to zero; positivity and the growth of the moment weights alone give no such bound. For comparison, the rational-value model in the companion paper has the same formal orders, leading coefficients and type of fixed-base power correction, although its target value is rational. The model and its denominator calculation are retained there with ordinary proofs as unformalised remarks. The companion paper also gives an ordinary argument for the ratio-limit extension under 𝑎𝑘+1/𝑎𝑘 →𝜌 ∈(0,𝑞−1)ak+1/ak→ρ∈(0,q−1), without the polynomial shift bound in Theorem 2.1. That extension remains unformalised.

A different question concerns the polynomial coefficients of the approximants, rather than their remainders. Van Assche’s little-𝑞q-Legendre construction [12] and the multiple-orthogonality construction of Postelmans and Van Assche [13] make the normalisation important. In the 2016 family, the companion paper proves positivity of the first matrix of a coefficient pencil for sizes 𝑁 ≤8N≤8, with real, interlacing roots below 𝐹(𝑝)F(p) for 𝑝 >1p>1. The shifted minors and coefficientwise positivity are supported by the stated finite polynomial computations. The coefficient-moment section gives the definitions and the precise ranges. Positivity for every 𝑁N and convergence of the largest root remain open. The general moment criteria of Wang and Zhu [15] and Sokal and Walrad [17], Berg’s factorial-power example [16], and the quadrature construction of Golub and Welsch [18] provide the relevant comparisons. Using a recurrence from another family would require a proof that it holds for these coefficients. The root-of-unity method of Krattenthaler, Rochev, Väänänen and Zudilin [14], for example, concerns a separate construction.

Congruences and divided forms

At 3/23/2, a polynomial 𝑄Q of degree at most 𝑊W has integral homogenised value 𝐻𝑊(𝑄) =2𝑊𝑄(3/2)HW(Q)=2WQ(3/2). Congruences at powers of 22 and 33 give finite counting criteria for combinations of such values. The companion paper treats integer rescaling and endpoint congruences and signed sums. It also treats the rank-one case and proves the quantitative finite-fibre estimate used below. Equal residues give a useful irrationality form only when the divided remainder is also nonzero and small. Smith normal form describes the image of the evaluated lattice [6], but does not estimate these real remainders.

For example, suppose that 𝑀M integral rows (𝐴𝑗,𝐵𝑗)(Aj,Bj) have remainders 𝑒𝑗 =𝐴𝑗𝐹(3/2) −𝐵𝑗ej=AjF(3/2)−Bj. Let 𝐷D be a positive integer, and suppose that the coefficient-pair subset sums ∑𝑗∈𝐼(𝐴𝑗,𝐵𝑗)∑j∈I(Aj,Bj) take 𝑄Q values in (ℤ/𝐷ℤ)2(Z/DZ)2. Put 𝑇 =∑𝑗|𝑒𝑗|T=∑j|ej| and suppose that at most 𝑘k subsets give any fixed remainder within a residue class. The least and greatest subset remainders are

∑𝑒𝑗<0𝑒𝑗and∑𝑒𝑗>0𝑒𝑗;∑ej<0ejand∑ej>0ej;

their difference is 𝑇T. Thus 𝑇T bounds the width of the range in each residue class as well. For each positive integer 𝑛n, the inequality

2𝑀>𝑄𝑘(⌊𝑛𝑇𝐷⌋+1)(16)(16)2M>Qk(⌊nTD⌋+1)

gives two subsets with the same residue vector whose remainder values differ by an amount strictly between 00 and 𝐷/𝑛D/n in absolute value. Indeed, in each residue class divide the range of remainders into half-open intervals of width 𝐷/𝑛D/n, starting at its least value. At most ⌊𝑛𝑇/𝐷⌋ +1⌊nT/D⌋+1 intervals are needed, including a last interval when the greatest value is an endpoint. If each interval contained only one remainder value, it would contain at most 𝑘k subsets, contrary to (16). Thus some interval contains two different remainder values; the half-open convention makes their separation strictly less than 𝐷/𝑛D/n. Subtracting the two subset sums and dividing their coefficients by 𝐷D gives an integral linear form of nonzero absolute value less than 1/𝑛1/n. The quantitative lemma and its proof state the finite-set version without assumptions about Lambert series.

The elementary integer-base method provides a different comparison. Vandehey [10] and Duverney and Tachiya [11] use integer-base expansions. At a noninteger rational base the cleared-tail recurrence has a growing denominator contribution. The clearing and tail-recurrence calculations in the companion paper include the coordinatewise obstruction at 3/23/2. They make no assertion about other approximation families. At the function level, Bell and Smertnig [9] exclude Mahler equations for the divisor generating series, while leaving the arithmetic of a single rational argument undecided.

A construction problem.

The unrestricted request for primitive polynomial rows and a signed combination whose divided remainder lies strictly between 00 and 1/𝑛1/n is equivalent to the irrationality of the target. The companion paper retains the full statement and proves this equivalence in its section on divided linear forms. A more specific question must prescribe the approximation family. For the 2004 family one can instead ask whether a parameter direction improves 𝜃∗θ∗. The all-base degree restriction proves an upper bound of 1/21/2 for the degree cutoff. Its hypotheses require one polynomial family, with common leading constants in its degree, coefficient-height and remainder estimates at every fixed real base 𝑥 >1x>1; the error terms may depend on 𝑥x. Merely having estimates at 3/23/2 does not suffice.

Under those hypotheses, the nondecay corollary goes beyond the failure of a sufficient criterion: after denominator clearing, the undivided forms cannot tend to zero at any rational base 𝑎/𝑏a/b with 𝑏 <𝑎 <𝑏2b<a<b2, including 3/23/2, even without a quadratic degree limit. If that limit exists, their absolute values tend to infinity in this strict region. Division by additional base-dependent content and families outside these hypotheses remain unclassified. Equality in the rational-base cutoff is also unresolved by the estimates of Section 4.

Verification and reproducibility

The evidence record indexes the existing Lean proofs and recorded Comparator comparisons at the source revision. Theorem 2.1 is the polynomial-bound specialisation of the geometric-moment proof cited in the companion paper; its Comparator association remains pending. The broader ratio-limit argument and rational-value model there have ordinary proofs only. This revision has had no fresh Lean or Comparator run and no independent review.

Data availability.

The cited source revision contains the Lean sources, toolchain and library manifest. The companion paper supplies the longer algebraic arguments and the precise scope of the finite computations.
